newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate does not cut off Bosnian troop funds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate does not cut off Bosnian troop funds.

text.p: The U.S. Senate on Friday strongly urged but did not require the United States to pull out its troops from Bosnia by next June 30, giving the White House the flexibility it sought for the peace-keeping mission.

The House has voted to cut off funds for the troops on June 30, 1998, despite Clinton administration arguments that a mandatory date could endanger U.S. troops, jeopardise their mission, and undermine U.S. credibility with its key European allies.
The House and Senate positions will have to be reconciled in a conference.

The nonbinding sense of the Senate amendment, offered by Michigan Democratic Sen. Carl Levin, passed on a voice vote on a bipartisan basis. It was part of a $268 billion defence spending bill which the Senate later passed easily on a 94-4 vote.

The Bosnia vote was a compromise that put the Senate firmly on record as seeking an end to U.S. military involvement within a year, but avoiding a confrontation with the administration or the Pentagon.
"United States ground combat forces should not participate in a follow-on force in Bosnia and Herzegovina after June 1998," the amendment said.
The Levin measure added that Western European allies should be on notice that they will have to step in with a follow-up force as necessary.

The amendment takes note that U.S. forces may play a supportive role in that European initiative. Levin later told reporters that could possibly include air, naval, logistics, communication or intelligence support. Ground troops could be in reserve nearby but would not be in Bosnia itself, he said.

Sen. Russell Feingold, a Wisconsin Democrat, had initially spearheaded an effort for a firmer cut-off date, saying without a deadline the "the mission absolutely risks continuing for who knows how long." But he ended up backing the Levin alternative, saying it did send the clear message that "it is time to bring our troops home."

President Bill Clinton also says he wants the troops out by mid-1998, but does not want U.S. hands tied in a way that could damage attempt to help create stability in Bosnia within the framework of the Dayton peace pact.

Gen. John Shalikashvili, chairman of the joint chiefs of staff, and Defence Secretary William Cohen, wrote in a letter made public on Friday that the cut-off would be a setback to efforts to break the four-year cycle of violence in the former Yugoslavia.

"A fixed withdrawal date will constrict U.S. commander's flexibility, encourage our opponents and undermine the important psychological advantage U.S. troops enjoy," they wrote Democratic Senate Leader Thomas Daschle of South Dakota.
"Legislative action of this nature on a matter of European security could very well undermine the cohesion of the NATO Alliance," they said.
A recent letter from the White House to Congress said a cut-off date could lead to a veto for the whole defence authorisation bill.
The administration also has concerns about some other elements of the bill, particularly the version passed by the House calling for more B-2 bombers that the Pentagon says it does not need or want.
